narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 53.1% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is just over 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year grades had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the second decile for Year 3 performance, noticeably below the average of about 5.8 among students who were accepted. This low ranking signaled to the model a higher risk that you might struggle with the bar exam.

Your undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction, modestly pulling the prediction toward passing. At 3.30, it sits slightly above the 3.23 average of accepted students, giving the model some reassurance about your academic ability.

Your LSAT score of 35 also nudged the outcome slightly toward success, though less strongly than your GPA. It is only a little below the 37.18 average of accepted applicants, so the model saw it as a mild positive but not enough to overcome the concern from your third-year class ranking.

Taken together, the model concluded your overall profile carried more than a 50% risk of bar failure, which triggered the rejection. To improve your chances next time, focus on strengthening your later-year academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. These two steps would most directly address the factors that weighed against you. (218 words)
